Understandability and Coherence.explanation: I think the story is successful as a unified whole. I can't say I understood the meaning of the end, and I was a bit confused about how the Bob Dylan lyric, and the European movie (which movie was being referenced), and the person's poem written for her all fit together. However, the reference to the sudden ending of the movie, and the sudden ending of the story were interesting and provocative. Some of the foreshadowing earlier in the story suggested that perhaps this trip wasn't going to end well (e.g. "Later, they would both show the cove photos to the people waiting for them at home, the wife and the husband. Or that’s what she imagined.").

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: I thought this story is successful; even though there isn't a lot of literary allusion or metaphor, some of the allusions are interesting. These include the reference to Girl from the North Country, as well as the repeated theme of photos the two took. I like this, because it suggests that the main things that will remain from the encounter between these two people are the photos. The line "that's the way I remember her best" comes to mind from the song, even though it isn't mentioned explicitly in the story. These references are subtle (I may even be imagining them!), but overall they create a very nice atmosphere, a sense that all the attempts of these two people to enjoy their time together is really not working, and that there is nothing really that will follow from it.

Narrative Ending.explanation: Of course, the ending is abrupt. But it is clearly by design, and I think it is successful. As I said earlier, I'm not sure if I understand the author's meaning completely, but the idea seems to be that these people's time together is fleeting, and will end, with nothing to follow.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: I think there is good balance between the stretching of time in the description of scenes, such as their swimming in the cove. Things that happened in the past are not compressed too much, and we get interesting details, such as the gentle chiding of the Europeans they meet, and the exasperation of the house manager.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The scenes are vivid, of ambiguous in their meaning. There is plenty of detail that helps the reader imagine the tension in the car as they drive to the beach, and the beer-drinking beachgoers in the distance even as the two main characters seem to be drifting apart from each other (literally and figuratively). I do think these scenes are balanced well with background information and exposition, which also include important details that fill in the gaps about the main characters, such as their imagined farewell at the station the next day.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The story kept me guessing along the way, but never became unbelievable within the context of the narrative. The author created a lot of tension, to the point that I imagined that something terrible might happen while the two were swimming at the cove. The fact that it didn't kept me wondering, and sustained the tension, right up until the end of the story.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: Although we do get some insights into the man's character that give him some depth, his perspective is mainly hidden from us. The sole perspective is really that of the woman.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Dialog and action is blended well with the main character's inner thoughts and interpretation about what is happening. This is effective, for example, when the two are apparently enjoying themselves at the beach, but she is actually longing for a beer from the other strangers.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: I thought the allusion to "certain European movies" that end suddenly, which then becomes the actual form of the story, was original and interesting.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I think the reader is left wondering about the meaning of the end of the story. It seems like there is an interesting idea here about how things end, whether they be art (e.g. films and short stories) or relationships. It made me think about the idea of what is "supposed" to happen in both. Art normally requires resolution (or at least, we expect resolution in art), and it is jarring when it is absent. And yet, in life, things pass unresolved all the time. Putting these two ideas together seems like an original and sophisticated idea.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story seems quite original and avoids cliche.

World Building and Setting.explanation: There are many sensory details that make this world believable and vivid. Some examples are: "He made a quick, nervous veer for an exit, her water bottle rolling off the dashboard"; "Some mornings, the wind knocked over the wicker furniture on the patio and blew tree branches onto the cracked tennis court and everyone stayed indoors, waiting silently for their turn at the Nespresso"; "Already the sun was drifting toward the ridge—it was later than she thought. She moved her towel to stay in the sun.

Character Development.explanation: I think both of the main characters are developed pretty well. The woman is more complex of a character, because we have her point of view. However, there are details about the man that give us some insight about him as well, for example, "I miss you, he’d write to her later, back in the States, though the nights she went to his room he was nervous and spoke to the ceiling and they mostly just talked and he seemed relieved when she crept back to her own room"; references to his basketball shoes and big American swimsuit.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There is rich subtext, as the main character seems continually conflicted about whether she wants to be where she is, doing what she is doing. On the surface, she is carefree, riding to the beach with the guy she met, skipping the ceramics and the museum, and whatever else. And yet, she is unhappy and unsatisfied, longing for a beer, imagining that if their relationship continued they would only hate each other. This tension is maintained throughout the story.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: This story was really incoherent, and felt like a kind of fever dream. Much of it did not make sense, and if we boil down the action, it is basically just two people standing together on the beach (with one occasionally laughing for no reason).

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: A lot of the language is just strange and nonsensical. Some such passages include "However, she managed to laugh louder and louder until her laughter transformed into an embrace of the sun's atmosphere"; "Her head melted back into her flip-flopped shoulders, and her joy seemed genuine and resounding. Del's surprise turned to heightened uncertainty, his footing unstable like the sand beneath his feet"; "He placed a wager against himself about the idea of diving past the sea-streaks of red-purple heavens and plunging into the sweet ache of burning pleasure that light-burn caused behind his peeled eyelids. The cold seagrass would attempt to wrap around his legs like a sea creature, hungry for attention, persistently gnawing and nibbling its way beneath him. Del smirked at the idea of a slight tinge of burning pee that no one would ever know was there except him.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending seems arbitrary, mainly because no significant action or conflict has taken place. The concluding idea is vague and doesn't really reveal anything about these characters: "Heather and Del continued to build memories, existing together in an intricate balance between wanting and fearing.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: Time is stretched much too thinly in this story, since nothing significant (or coherent) seems to happen.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation:
There is a balance between scene and exposition, and we have a blending of dialog with narrator's commentary. There are a couple of passages where the dialog is (inadvertently I suspect) very funny. I laughed out loud at this passage: "Heather's voice exuded warmth like the sun they'd been watching, as she replied softly, "I imagine the sun sinking into the sea, like melting gold flowing into its lover's embrace."

Del considered her words while still standing idly with uncertainty and a hint of suspicion. A malicious inner turmoil forced him to confront the gnawing question of whether to maintain his doubts or to give in to that spark of romanticism. Did she mean the sun melting the water and evaporating it, boiling the ocean's organisms into a state of life-extinction, or drying up the world until it became nothing but black sores of star-dust and cosmic desolation?

Del shifted on his knees and glanced down at his toes, where bits of seafoam playfully tickled the wet hairs. Dismissing his skepticism, he stifled his anxieties and decided to accept it as a poetic image. Putting on a brave smile, he said, "That's beautiful."
If intended as comedy, it is great, Del is utterly unaware about Heather's romantic take on the situation, has no idea what she is talking about, and yet manages to say something obliquely romantic as well. Was comedy the intention of the author (or the artificial intelligence that produced this)? I'm not sure.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: Although the things that happen in the story are utterly strange, they aren't appropriate, and just seem nonsensical.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The main perspective is that of Del, and there isn't much in the way of Heather's perspective.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Much of the narrative seems to be the interior thoughts and interpretation of Del. There isn't a lot of action happening in this story.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: There isn't anything original about form or structure.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I don't imagine the reader will come away with any unique or original idea. I could not really make much sense of what the takeaway would be. There is little in the way of conflict, character development, and it is not even really clear what the story is about.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The problem isn't that the story relies on cliches as much as the language is convoluted and doesn't make much sense. An example is this passage: "Beachside, with the night young and Heather's chest filled with an innocuous laugh, he felt a renewed sense of hope. Time never seemed to move more slowly than when it kept pace with Heather's thoughts, all woven and adorned with the very shades of fascination that clung to their seaside forms.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The world does not seem real, instead the story evoked a dream where everything was kind of strange and a little off. There are elements of the real world, but they are arranged in a way where they don't quite fit together properly.

Character Development.explanation: The characters are not developed in any sophisticated way. They say things and react in ways that don't seem realistic.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There doesn't seem to be much of any meaning, either on the surface or below it.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: Much of the story is vague, and so it is difficult to become invested in the lives of the characters. What were the challenges they faced at the beginning to be together? Why was their love story so extraordinary? The second half of the story goes on and on and repeats the same ideas: art brought them together and their love endured. It is not a very interesting or satisfying story.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story doesn't make very sophisticated use of language, which is often vague. Metaphors tend to be commonplace and not very effective. For example, "their love matured like fine wine"; "Sarah's hand found its place in Max's, threads of connection once again intertwined." There is a lot of weaving, intertwining, and etching going on, in a way that feels repetitive.

Narrative Ending.explanation: Nothing really happens after the characters reunite, and so the ending is basically "they stayed together in love until they died.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The chronology after they reunite is both vague and drawn out, so we don't get many interesting details, and yet the text continues for much longer than it needs to.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There is more narrator exposition, and some more scenes with dialog between the characters would help to give them some depth.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The main "twist" in the story is that Sarah and Max reunite, which is appropriate to the narrative, but not all that surprising. After that, there are no further conflicts or significant events.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The main point of view is that of the narrator, who treats Max and Sarah's points of view as virtually interchangeable. We don't really understand their differences as individuals.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: It would help if there was more action happening, and more detail about what conflict was involved in Max and Sarah being together. What was at stake, what did they overcome?

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: There isn't anything original about the form and structure.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: There is not really anything for the reader to sink their teeth into here. Max and Sarah meet, they can't stay together for some reason, then they reunite and can be together for some reason, and then they stay together happily until they die. There doesn't seem to be much meaning beyond this.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story avoids cliche for the most part; the main problem with the language is that it is vague, we don't have any details that make the characters interesting or worth caring about.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The world feels very two-dimensional. There is a beach, a sunset, a studio, but not much beyond these vague outlines of physical reality. Even the dog feels random, and not really connected to anything else in the world or the story.

Character Development.explanation: Both characters seem flat and not very developed. We don't know anything about their back story, their history together, or what distinguishes them from each other.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There doesn't seem to be any meaning or complexity below the surface narrative.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story is coherent, and each action leads logically to the next. We understand the circumstances of this trip to the beach, some of the back story, and the impermanence which is at the heart of the story.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story does not make sophisticated use of these devices, but at the same time the simplicity of the language is not necessarily a weakness. Where metaphors are used, they are not brilliant, but also not awkward or over the top. For example, " She felt anchored to him by invisible threads, being reeled in bit by bit with each furtive look across the mess hall.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending feels natural. We know that this is the final chance these two have to be together, and that they have to go their separate ways. It thus feels appropriate to the story.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing feels appropriate, the story is told over the course of a day, with Jane's memories filling in the blanks in the past to help the reader understand the history between these two. Nothing feels too drawn out or compressed. Two paragraphs are repeated in their entirety, which I assume is not intended.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There is also good balance between action in the scenes playing out on this particular day, scenes from the past, revealed through Jane's memories, and summary based on her memories (for example, "He had been quietly confident, making wry observations about the eccentric group of creatives thrown together in communal living. His sardonic humor and reticent thoughtfulness had drawn her in immediately. However, her shyness held her back from striking up a conversation with him that night."). The scenes would be improved by more specific detail in the dialog between the two during their time together. For example, this paragraph would be improved with more specific detail: "Jane opened up extensively about her work, her past, her family, and her hopes while Mark listened intently, drawing out more details with his astute questions. She was surprised by their easy rapport, how fully she felt seen and how at ease she felt opening up to Mark. He recounted amusing anecdotes from past relationships, travel misadventures, eccentric neighbors and life in the city. His wry observations and witty stories kept her spellbound throughout the long, golden afternoon.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There are not really any surprising turns in the narrative. However, the story does build tension through Jane's thoughts about Mark, both in her memories at the artist residency, and in the car and at the beach on this day.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: We seem to have Jane's perspective exclusively. Mark is something of a cipher for her thoughts.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: I think there is a good balance between Jane's thoughts and interpretation of events, and the events and action themselves. Again, some more detail in the dialog at the beach would help to give more depth to both characters.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: There isn't really anything original about the form and structure.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I think the reader comes away a bit disappointed by the story overall. There is enough detail about the events leading up to this day, and about the tension that exists between the two people, so the reader is. invested in them and what happens. Furthermore, the ending is not inappropriate, since we know this relationship must end. However, a further turn of the narrative, or something revealed about either of them during the trip to the beach would make the story more satisfying. As it is now, there is not much of an original idea for the reader to chew on.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story does seem original, and avoids cliches.

World Building and Setting.explanation: There are good details about the physical world that help to make it believable. Some examples include: "Jane gripped the sun-cracked vinyl seat, glancing over at Mark behind the wheel. His brow was furrowed, focused on navigating the treacherous turns through the coastal fog. The radio played softly, an old jazz tune Jane vaguely recognized filling the silence between them"; "The Dodge emerged from the woods into a sandy clearing. The fog parted to reveal the wide blue ocean stretched endlessly before them, azure waters lapping at ivory sands"; "The chilled water was bracing, raising goosebumps on her bare skin.

Character Development.explanation: Jane's character is pretty well developed, but Mark seems very two-dimensional. There is an opportunity for the reader to learn more about him during their time together in the car or at the beach, but the story doesn't develop in this way.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There is not much development of themes below the surface of the main narrative, i.e. that these two are attracted to each other, and even though we wonder how it will play out, we know it will end. There is not much in the way of subtext beyond this.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: This is an excellent, expertly-written short story. The author doles out information in a stingy, deliberate, highly satisfying way. By initially withholding crucial information - who the protagonist is, what their relationship fully is to their partner, where exactly they are and why - the author induces curiosity in the reader; through skillful revelation and implication these questions are answered and hinted at wonderfully. This is a lean, textured, and viscerally human piece of fiction in which every thought, utterance, and detail adds to the reader's enjoyment.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: idiomatic language like "People must have acted dumb," "apron of concrete" (this might also be construed as metaphor, but apron in this context is also an idiom for the entrance to a driveway), "doggy-paddled" adds nuance and complexity and meaning to the text. Through the use of such language the author deepens the readers understanding of the characters' (in particular the unnamed female protagonist's) relationship to the environment they are vacationing in (presumably Spain).

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending of this piece is outstanding; its lack of resolution is clearly appropriate and earned. The entire story builds towards this moment of open-ended dissatisfaction and comparison between the protagonist's affair partner and a previous, more satisfying one (who is, evidently and importantly, not her current husband). It is a deeply nuanced and moving moment of interiority and humanity in which the reader uses what they have learned and inferred throughout the story to fill in the gaps. The fact that we leave the story in a state of unresolve and longing for more artfully simulates the subjective experience of the story's protagonist.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story begins in media res, which is to say in the middle of the action, plunging the reader into a situation that must be deciphered by the reader. We experience this intimate scene at a languorous, appropriate pace before zooming into the conditional future, learning things that the protagonist does not yet know, creating a resonant dramatic irony. This adds meaning, depth, and context to the piece's open-ended conclusion.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The future moments conveyed in the first three paragraphs of this story's third page (later referenced to as "the next day") comes in a more summary, expository mode than the rest of the piece, which unfolds in scene with brief dips into further-past exposition. All of this is additive to the story.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: This story is full of fascinating revelations and turns, largely created by the author's masterful use of narrative withholding. We are constantly learning new things that add meaning and context - that the protagonist and the man who initially appears to be her boyfriend or husband are each married to other people, that they meet at the residency as opposed to having gone there together, that she is significantly older than him... These revelations keep the reader immersed and engaged throughout the piece.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The protagonist, clearly, is beautifully rendered. We understand her to the degree and in the fashion that one understands oneself - which is to say, both intimately and not nearly enough. She feels complex and human because of, not in spite of, her contradictions. Similarly, her partner, who we minimally understand through her perspective, feels like a human being that one has just met and whom we can't decide whether we respect or not. Reading him through the protagonist's perspective feels startingly true to life.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: This piece does an incredible job of balancing interiority with exteriority. Its use of free indirect speech ("people must have acted dumb all the time," "would either of them mention this was the wrong beach?" "this is the part where - ") to convey the protagonist's thoughts creates an intimate, subjective, and immersive reading experience. We experience what the protagonist does as though we are the protagonist, despite the story being told in the third person.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation:
This piece excels on both the line and form levels. The author makes unconventional decisions, like eliding quotation marks around dialogue, that create artful and immersive effects. The reader has to slow down and think in order to understand whether statements are dialogue or thought, and if so, whose. Grammatical structures like comma and em dash usage create complex, idiosyncratic sentences. Clauses are connected in ways that convey causal and contextual meaning. 

Example: They'd brought beers and an opener and towels from the residency to that first beach-the house manager had been angry.

In that sentence, list-like repetition of the conjunction 'and,' coupled with the specificity of "that first beach," implies an amount of effort that contrasts with the absence of and protagonist's desire for beer at "their last beach," at which the story mainly takes place. Connecting the independent clause "the house manager had been angry" with an em dash to this list implies a bewildering causal relationship that is explained in the following sentence. Reading this sentence meaningfully *feels* like it would to be the protagonist, only realizing that she had committed an infraction after the fact.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: This story places us into the headspace of a specific woman experiencing something highly personal to her. Yet what she yearns for - human connection, freedom, release - are universal wants. Feeling these desires through her unique perspective induces contemplation and empathy in the reader.

Originality in Thought.explanation: This language in this story is fresh and conveyed with originality. For example, the universal experience of being so different from others in a new environment as to feel alien is expressed in a fresh and specifically detailed way in the single-sentence second paragraph of the third page: Some mornings, the wind knocked over the wicker furniture on the patio and blew tree branches onto the cracked tennis court and everyone stayed indoors, waiting silently for their turn at the Nespresso, and that's when she looked around and thought, Who are these people?

World Building and Setting.explanation: Though this piece is spare with description, its details are specific and skillfully chosen. The sentence noted in the previous answer is a strong example of the author's world-building ability.

Character Development.explanation: The protagonist is a complex, challenging, real-feeling woman, full stop. Her depth of feeling and observations, and her contradictory contempt for her affair partner (and perhaps herself) absolutely mirrors the complexity of a real person.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: This piece has an iceberg of subtext floating underneath it. The entire story is conveyed through the successful integration of subtext and text. The interactions between the protagonist and the man (Did you see me jump of the rock? No, she hadn't. Did he notice she had gone in the water too, that her hair was dripping? No, he hadn't.)convey a profound disconnect that causes the reader to wonder why the protagonist continues to suffer the presence of this man she clearly disdains and seems to view as an incompetent man-child.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: This piece is so...adjacent to being coherent. It seems to be obsessed with conveying poetic-seeming imagery that doesn't actually make sense. There is no character arc to speak of, but rather an abrupt asserted resolution that does not connect logically from what came before. The descriptions of Del and Heather's actions, and Del's thought's specifically, feel like an alien describing human beings without having encountered one.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: This piece goes wildly overboard with attempts at metaphor and figurative language that only occasionally approaches meaning. The sea is obsessively and meaninglessly described as a variety of colors "as though a whole tanker of oil had been spilled on the water," wading closer "in an attempt to absorb the last of the blues and the oranges and the purples and the reds into a wild dance of harmony and discord at the same time." Frequently this language is explicitly explained to the reader: "a love story etched in both the shifting sands and the transient waves, forever a testament to the mosaic of emotions they crafted together as one.

Narrative Ending.explanation: I do not understand what transpired to cause this pat, overly-resolved conclusion in which Del and Heather come together as one. This story is baffling overall, making it difficult to make sense of what actually happened at all, let alone how the conclusion connects to the rest of it. It's essentially a "happily ever after" ending that is simply asserted rather than derived from what came before.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The piece unfolds as one long scene in which things happen almost randomly. Del answers questions that were never posed to him. There is no compression or stretching of time to speak of.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: This story is one 21-paragraph scene onto which a summary and expository ending is appended without perceptible cause.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The surprsing things that happen in this piece are surprsing because they are random and nonsensical. Del smirks at the tinge of his secret, burning pee? He tells Heather that he always wanted a fish for a pet, answering a question that is not present in the text?

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: There are two characters in this piece, and both do and say things that make no sense. They are not understandable as human beings.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: We frequently dip into Del's interiority, but the things he thinks are confounding. When Heather says she's thinking about "the sun sinking into the sea, like melting gold flowing into its lover's embrace," (an unlikely thing for a human being to say), Del wonders if she means that she's thinking about the sun literally sinking into the sea and extinguishing all of the life within it, and this thought is expressed in almost erotic figurative phrasing. It's bizarre.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation:
There are occasional uses of unconventional sentence structure: 

She glanced at the water-a splash of blue-or the sand-a gentle brush-or the sky-a sea of blank space holding together this delicately balanced world-and found nothing to distract her gaze. 

However, this odd grammar does not read as intentional, and the idea being expressed seems self-contradictory. To the extent that one's gaze can be "distracted," isn't that exactly what's being described by that list of sights?

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: This story seems to be affixed to a romantic, painterly depiction of this couple's relationship, but in a way that doesn't seem to make a lot of sense. The themes of color, sun, sea life, and sand are obsessively adhered to without saying much at all.

Originality in Thought.explanation: This story says a lot of original things, but they are incoherent. What are "flip-flopped shoulders"? It uses imagery from a set of themes (color, sun, sea life, sand) in a rigid, obsessive, Terminator-like fashion without seeming to understand what the words actually mean.

World Building and Setting.explanation: This world of this story is hard to understand on a basic level. "Sea-streaks of red-purple heavens"? "Tiny flecks of sand that had bitten her feet for the past nineteen days"?

Character Development.explanation: These characters are difficult to conceive of as real human beings. They consistently behave in bizarre, erratic ways that are vaguely adjacent to, but discordant with, actual human behavior.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation:
This story reads as almost deliberately opposed to subtext. The nonsensical actions, statements, and thoughts of its characters are frequently explained directly to the reader:

"I did always want one of those fish as a pet," Del finally answered...although he had said that, he knew he didn't actually want one-it was merely a measure of whimsy masquerading as a deep desire.

That is a typical selection from this piece, in which things that don't make sense are followed by meticulous explanations that are themselves confusing.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: This is a superficial piece of writing in which flat caricatures of human beings behave in rote, simplistic ways. It attempts to end in a long series of oddly similar paragraphs that circle narrative closure but never land in a meaningful manner.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The language in this piece is overly-familiar and trite, with actions described the way one has seen a million times before. Sarah "gathers her thoughts," "takes a deep breath," and "tucks a stray strand of hair behind her ear and avoids meeting Max's gaze." If these phrasings were not so firmly embedded in the culture they would be examples of plagiarism.

Narrative Ending.explanation:
The summary and abrupt ending goes on and on in an agonizing series of attempted conclusions, each of which follows the same formula of an initial time-setting clause attached to a trite attempt at poetic description, followed by a "happily ever after"-style conclusion.

Ex: "As the night deepened, and the stars sprinkled across the sky, they made their way back to the residency. Every step they took was slow and deliberate, their hands occasionally brushing against each other, but the weight of their imminent departures loomed between them.

In the days that followed, time seemed to slip through their fingers like the sand on the beach. Sarah found solace in her art, pouring her emotions into each brushstroke, while Max immersed himself in the solitude of his studio, weaving his experiences into the very fabric of his creations.

Finally, the day of their departure arrived. Tear-filled farewells were exchanged, along with promises to stay in touch. With heavy hearts, Sarah and Max bid the residency town adieu and boarded separate flights to their respective homes.

Months passed, filled with missed calls and unanswered messages. Life's demands had reclaimed their attention, and the ephemeral relationship they had built on that beach seemed like a distant memory. Yet, in the quiet moments of the night, Sarah and Max found themselves inexplicably drawn back to that special place, their hearts forever tethered by the bonds they had shared."

This move repeats over and over, and in fact makes up the majority of the text.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: While the story does attempt stretching and compression of time, it is done in an incoherent, unbalanced manner that does not read as intentional. The above answer is an example of what I mean.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The scenes in this story are simplistically rendered, and the summary/expository attempts at an ending are not believable.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: This story articulates a flat, simplistic understanding of human life that seems devoid of the complicated actions and thoughts of real human beings. There are no "turns" to speak of.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation:
The characters are rendered in a flat, caricatured fashion in which their every thought and action is explicitly explained away, even though these thoughts and actions are transparent. 

Ex: Taking a deep breath, Sarah gathered her thoughts, searching for the right words to express the swirling turmoil within her. "We've been avoiding the inevitable, Max," she finally said, her voice tinged with traces of sadness. "During our time here, we've grown closer, and now that it's almost over, we can't just pretend like it never happened."

Max's eyes softened, his hand gently reaching for hers. "I understand, Sarah," he whispered, his voice filled with a mixture of comprehension and sorrow. "But how do we move forward? How do we navigate this complexity without unraveling everything we've built?

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: There is little to no meaningful interiority in this story.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: This is an algorithmic approach to storytelling that follows a set of rigid moves and sentence structure. The one original move, the odd 2.5 pages of repeated attempts at an ending, cannot be intentional.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: The themes and content of this story are overly-familiar and derivative. There is nothing to take away from it, because it does not convey an understanding of human feeling or thought.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The language of this piece is full of cliches. "Their love matured like fine wine," "they strolled...hand-in-hand," "they remembered...the stolen kisses." Virtually all of the turns of phrase in this piece can be found elsewhere, and presumably were.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The descriptive language of this piece is vague and straightforward. The town is repeatedly described as "idyllic," for example, rather than that meaning being conveyed through subtle and artful use of language.

Character Development.explanation:
The characters are rendered in too flat and simplistic a manner for them to feel real or complex. The things they say are literal and devoid of human-like meaning:

"Perhaps it's enough to acknowledge what we feel, to cherish these moments we've shared without putting unnecessary labels on it." 

"I can do that, Sarah. As long as we're on the same page, as long as we understand that this is a space we've carved out for ourselves, separate from the rest of our lives.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: This story is superficial and goes out of its way to avoid subtext and explain every thing away, even though those things are obvious at a grade-school level.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story repeats itself several times in an attempt to satisfy its prompt, creating an illogical path in which Jane says and thinks the same things, typically in the exact same language. Other times, it seems to 'forget' what has already been established, so that we are told that Jane feels self-conscious in her swimsuit under Mark's appreciative gaze (thus, we know he can see her in her swimsuit) only to slip off her sundress (a contradiction) in the next moment with Mark once again gazing on her appreciatively.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The language in this piece is littered with trite, familiar phrases. "brow was furrowed," "pangs of longing," "tucked away in the woods," "lingering glances," "furtive looks," "stolen moments," etc. All of these expressions, when used by human writers, are employed thoughtlessly because they are so familiar as to almost autocomplete in the mind.

Narrative Ending.explanation: Like the 3rd story, this one falls into a circular pattern halfway through, though not to the same extent. However, the story exists on such a superficial plane, in which the characters are static and simple, that the ending just sort of happens. There isn't much to resolve in this piece. The characters begin it knowing that their time together will end soon and end it aware that there time together is ending.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: Aside from the circular algorithmic trap that the story falls into, its story time is nearly static. There is no meaningful stretching, lingering, or compression of time.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation:
There are only the thinnest whisps of scene in this story. Rather, the reader is told what happened and how, then has why what happened matters explained away:

"Jane felt the residency was ending too quickly. Over the past month, she had started and scrapped three paintings, unable to focus because of her preoccupation with Mark. Her thoughts kept drifting to his dark eyes, his deliberate way of considering a question before answering, the glimpses of humor he allowed to surface when recounting some absurdist tale of life in the city. She felt anchored to him by invisible threads, being reeled in bit by bit with each furtive look across the mess hall. The hushed, intimate dinners they had shared, making eye contact across the worn farm table, left her breathless in a way she hadn't felt for years.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There are no meaningful or surprising turns in this story. The things that happened are predictable, obvious, and deliberately explained to the reader. it operates as though the reader is oblivious.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: There is no dialogue in this piece, so what the characters say is painstakingly expressed through reported speech: "Mark asked Jane about her own work. She explained her use of dramatic colors and abstractions to convey emotion, while he nodded thoughtfully." Rather than diving into their mindsets, we are simply told what they said and did, and generally, why. They are flat, simple approximations of human beings.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: This story is told through Jane's interiority and subjective experience, but in a simplistic, summary fashion. She does not believably reflect a human understanding of the world.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: This story proceeds in a  lumbering, rote, paint-by-numbers "this happened, then this happened, then this happened" manner. Outside of its odd loops of repeated ideas, it shows no originality in form or structure. The language is basic grade school prose.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: This is a flat, derivative piece that contains no meaningful ideas.

Originality in Thought.explanation: As indicated in some of my previous answers, the language of this piece is highly derivative, filled with basic analogies and phrasings.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The world is simplistically rendered. The beach is "sandy," the cliffside road is "winding," Jane's studio is "isolated." Basic, rote descriptions. Because the story only vaguely hints at scene, there isn't really an opportunity for it to build a complex, unique, or believable world for its characters to inhabit.

Character Development.explanation: The characters are flat, simple, automatons. They are too shallow to feel real.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: This story lacks subtext altogether, though to a less aggressive degree than stories 2 and 3.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story follows a couple who is growing apart as they try to find a specific beach. Their house manager is upset with them because of their mess and beer, and the trip to the beach (the wrong beach, not the one they were trying to find) results in the woman feeling lonely as the man goes for a swim. There's a gap in their ages that the woman feels self-conscious about. The man says he misses her once she goes back to the states, and as they're driving back, before she's gone, the woman listens to a Johnny Cash song that resonates with her. All of these elements work to emphasize the couple's parting and the fleeting nature of relationships, elements which the prose mirrors in its sparse matter-of-factness.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story uses an ocean and the lost beach as an extended metaphor for people growing apart and ending up in the wrong places. The parting trains also serve as a metaphor and allusion to the inevitable parting of the lines of people's lives, but all of these devices are used subtly enough to feel earned and refined.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The story's ending seems inevitable in that we know the man and woman are growing apart, and that the woman feels nostalgic and lonely by the story's end. The couple's parting is bittersweet and the ideas about other towns etc. allude to perhaps other futures the couple could have had. I loved the last line "This is the part where--" which ended with unusual punctuation and another potential ambiguous situation, which mirrors the themes of the story.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story has a dreamlike vacation quality to it, which makes sense as the couple is on vacation. The story's use of this hazy, dreamlike quality works with the ambiguous situation the couple is in with each other, as well as the slowness and strangeness of departures.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: This story is mostly in-scene which is great and doesn't seem to drag. The use of summary adds to the narrative momentum (i.e. description of the towns, the house manager, etc)., allowing the scenes to achieve maximum impact.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: Yes; the couple's parting is inevitable but the change in focus from the beach to the car to the trains is beautiful and surprising. I fell in love with the language and style of the stream-of-consciousness/associative logic of the piece.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The woman is an interesting character whose POV we dive deep into, but the man's perspective is more ambiguous. This seems to be a typical white couple on vacation which is fine and I don't think the man's perspective is really important to this story, which is more about the woman, but yeah the narrators weren't really diverse.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Yes! We see a lot of the woman's interiority re: what she thinks of her fleeting relationship with this younger man, and we also see a lot of external action re: the search for the beach, swimming, the car, parting etc. The woman's associative logic makes following her interiority in the way that it relates to her external circumstances interesting, and I enjoyed the way the two interacted smoothly.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: Not really until the ending. However, I don't think this story's narrative structure needed to be very original (this story seemed to be more about meaning/vignette than innovative structure, which was fine, as I feel like this structure was right for this piece).

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Yes! I think an average reader will be able to think about loss and parting and the ways in which different aspects of life and time enact this.

Originality in Thought.explanation: This story used some cliches (trains as symbols for parting, the ocean) but analyzed them in a way that felt fairly fresh. I think a story's power comes from its ability to describe how a moment feels for a specific person in a specific moment in time, which this story achieved. I felt like the narrative felt true and personal, which allowed me to resonate with it.

World Building and Setting.explanation: Yes! The landscape of the house, the beach, and the car felt lived-in and truthful. I could feel the warmth and graininess of the beach, as well as the coldness of alienation.

Character Development.explanation: Both characters are actually quite static, in that they don't change, but I think the story wasn't one that was centered around growth and internal change, rather, the inevitability of loss and nostalgia. Therefore, this story felt appropriate in its scope re: internal arcs but the characters weren't particularly dynamic.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Yes!!!!! Again, the idea of the story was fairly simple (the inevitability of age, parting, change), but it was illustrated in a way that felt inspiring re: questioning how these ideas relate and resonate throughout our own lives. It was really beautiful and I was left feeling changed at the end of it :)

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story used lots of adjectives and images that didn't really make sense or felt weird; i.e. "enigmatic horizon," "feeling the extended yet gentle silence between them" etc. and also felt too on-the-nose in its descriptions of people's emotions. The story was melodramatic with little sublety, and I found it to be a bit cringe-worthy.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story's descriptions were really overdone, with lots of adjectives piled on or weird images created that didn't really make sense. I found myself losing interest the more of these came up, and thought a bit more subtlety or ambiguity could make the story more interesting.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending didn't really make a lot of sense, with Del and Heather "building memories" together for an ambiguous amount of time after the story's end. It just felt like nothing really happened in the story and that nothing had really changed between them.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story's sense of time seemed to really encompass one day, but so much time was spent over-explaining Del and Heather's emotions that I quickly lost interest. I would have wanted to know more about inner lives that didn't feel really contrived.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: I think the scene-summary balance was okay but none of the scenes or summary were interesting. I think the writing style just really threw me and I had a hard time actually understanding what the point of it was. There was too much concrete interiority that was too easily resolved by the characters just forgetting about what they were worried about.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The story didn't really have any turns or surprises. As such, I can't really say any of the non-turns were appropriate.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The characters were really weird in that I didn't understand how they were working despite their emotions being described so explicitly. Heather says: "I imagine the sun sinking into the sea, like melting gold flowing into its lover's embrace" which causes Del confusion; he overanalyzes the statement but it's such a bad sentence that I don't know what to even think. Then, Del "smiles bravely" which also doesn't make sense. I think the characters just didn't really make any sense narratively so I didn't feel engaged by their perspectives.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Again, the characters interiority didn't make any sense. Externally, Del kept thinking about "invasive species" at random times, for no reason and without explanation. I don't think their interactions with the external world made much sense.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The story followed a straightforward structure but nothing happened in the story except for them walking. It didn't really feel like a story in that it didn't really have a clear progression from beginning to end.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I honestly think that the average reader, like me, would be bewildered by this story and not moved by it because of the fact that the characters emotions don't make sense and because the story doesn't really have a beginning, middle, and end. it doesn't really feel like a story.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story managed to be both cliche and emotionally indecipherable despite the over explanation of emotions. Lines about the sun being golden or "Before his lips could reach hers, Heather burst into peals of laughter. At first, it seemed like a prelude to a warning, a gesture that she could stand and leave him there alone on the shore to wallow in his misguided affection. However, she managed to laugh louder and louder until her laughter transformed into an embrace of the sun's atmosphere." I really did not understand what the writer was thinking here.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story does seem to be set at a beach and that is successful in that I knew where the characters were. The atmosphere was a bit weak since so much of the story was spent focusing on indecipherable internality of characters.

Character Development.explanation: As I have said quite a few times, the emotional narratives of the characters don't make sense as they behave kind of randomly and easily forget about their conflicts once someone laughs or something.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: The language was really bad and I don't really understand what was going on between the two characters. Things resolve way too easily by the end and I felt really confused by the story's character and narrative decisions.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: This story made a lot more sense than the last one in that Sarah and Max had a clear problem: their residency ending, and a a clear desire to somehow reunite with each other. I don't think the story was great, but it did follow a cohesive narrative.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story's descriptions were simplistic and childlike in a way that made the story kind of boring to read. There wasn't really any metaphor or any work being done at the language level to make the story have nuanced meaning. Essentially, Sarah and Max become successful artists but still remember their residency experience (which typically takes place during mid-career of an artist's life) so that doesn't quite add up. The story was told so plainly that I found myself really wanting for something more interesting to be done at the language level.

Narrative Ending.explanation: Sarah and Max die while thinking about their beach trip. I think my problem with the ending mainly has to do with problems involving the scope and pace of the story: the story follows Max and Sarah from the middle of their lives to the end of their lives, and time passes far too quickly for this to be interesting. The characters are one dimensional and only think about their beach residency which doesn't seem quite believable. They die also thinking of this residency rather than any other complexity within their relationship or in their lives.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing of this story is way too fast, following Sarah and Max in summary from their middle to late lives. I's hard to know exactly how old Sarah and Max are when the story begins, and they don't seem to really do anything other than make art and think about their residency for their whole lives.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The story was basically all summary after Sarah and Max meet the dog. Time moves too quickly and without any significant problems that change them or help them grow.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The story has no turns and instead just follows a couple as they happily pursue art with no difficulty while still remembering this one beach residency that they met at. The story is predictable and uninteresting as a result.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The characters only think about loving each other and their beach residency. Because they experience no problems, the characters read as flat and unrealistic.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: The characters really had no interiority. The story is mostly a summary of their successful art careers and their nostalgia for their beach residency.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The story moves too fast and while it makes sense in a beginning, middle, end sense, the characters experience no complications, which makes for a pretty boring read. There was really no tension in the story even in the beginning when they knew they were parting.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: The story wasn't memorable because it did not provide any new insight due to the scope of the characters wants and narratives. We also didn't learn anything about the art they were making or why they were making it, which made the story seem very vague and unoriginal.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story just had no problems that occurred within it and Max and Sarah had no personalities. There weren't really any cliches but the story just really didn't have anything going on within it; it felt very generic.

World Building and Setting.explanation: We can at least see the beach residency the characters go to, as well as the galleries and studio spaces. While sparsely described, at least they are existing in physical spaces.

Character Development.explanation: Again, the characters have no depth as they only think about how they are happy and that they are nostalgic for their beach residency. The characters don't grow at all from the time they meet to the time they die, and they are very preoccupied with this one residency for some reason which doesn't make narrative sense.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: No, as I have said, the characters have no internality as they only care about their residency and encounter zero problems. There is no subtext as there is nothing to have subtext about. I think the characters need to have more depth and desire.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: I found the story unsatisfying as it was written entirely in summary and I didn't really understand Jane as a character outside of her interest in Mark. She's at an artist residency, but we don't learn about her art, and she's kind of a flat and boring character. Nothing really happens to threaten her relationship with him within the span of the story; there are two days left in the residency but we don't really know what happens after, and there is no dialogue.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: There are no metaphors or interesting images within the story. Characters are clearly defined and there is little ambiguity of originality in rhythm or phrasing.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The story doesn't feel like it ends at the right place; because it ends before the residency ends, or because any tension occurred, it just felt like it ended before it was supposed to be done and that the author became tired and just ended it before the story's natural conclusion.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing was fine in that the story really took place two days before the residency was supposed to end, but I don't think the story started or ended at the right time because the story lacked the tension of time running out even when that was supposed to be the primary problem. However, the timing of the actual narrative made sense.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The story was completely in summary, with no dialogue or scene. As a result, I didn't feel close to the characters or embodied within the world. I would recommend adding more scenes so that the story is at least 70% scene to 30% summary (a more ideal balance).

Structural Flexibility.explanation: This story had no turns so I wasn't able to be surprised by anything within it. The narrator is basically just really into Mark for some reason (we don't actually get to know anything about his character), and doesn't do anything about it. Then the story ends.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: Again, the narrator really had nothing interesting going on in her head. She was interested in Mark and worried about what would happen because the residency was ending, but didn't act on that desire or have any complex thoughts on it.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: The narrator's interiority was basically just about her being interested in Mark and nervous that the residency was ending. I didn't feel like anything insightful was being said and was therefore unmoved by the story and left wanting for more interiority that had greater insight on the world.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The story was structurally linear and thus unoriginal. I actually don't think stories need to be original in terms of form and structure to be successful; most stories actually follow similar structures; it's more about whether or not a story's structure makes sense for it and allows the story to achieve maximum effect. That being said, this story's scope was too narrow both in terms of time and Jane's "want" which was pretty much to start a relationship with Mark even though we really don't know how he feels at all. The story could have spend more time in-scene with their interactions as well as what is at stake for Jane if she is unable to make this relationship work.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Because Jane's want is so narrow, I was unable to really resonate with any of the themes. As a queer person, maybe that's just because this is a white straight narrative, but I also think it's because I didn't really know anything about Jane and her art or what about Mark was so interesting to her. As such, the story was flat and uninspiring.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story felt generic in that it was about a person who was wanting a person and worrying about time running out. It didn't execute this concept interestingly and thus fell flat.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The setting of the beach, car, and ocean were a lot more clear here than in the past two stories; I liked the detail about the car's color and vibe, as well as the temperature of the water and the sun.

Character Development.explanation: Jane doesn't grow at all from the beginning to the end; she simply desires Mark and then doesn't do anything about it. There's not really anything that happens internally that she realizes or finds meaning in.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Again, because Jane's want was so simple, there was nothing that could really be taken from this story. I wanted the story to say something more meaningful about life or art, but the story was too consumed with Jane's crush (we also didn't know why she had this crush or anything about Mark).
